newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Millennium bug threatens computer chaos.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Millennium bug threatens computer chaos.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
The information superhighway looks like facing some major roadworks and serious hold-ups with the turn of the millennium.
Experts have assured us that computers would make our lives fuller and easier. Entertainment, shopping, education and communications would all be enhanced by computing.

Many mundane number-crunching tasks have already been taken over by these ubiquitous machines. Computers control activities such as credit card transactions, banking, global air traffic movements and nuclear power plant cooling.
But the millennium bug threatens to undermine all this.
As clocks tick past midnight on December 31, 1999, many computers across the world will either crash or start pumping out erroneus data.
Considering the resources and brainpower in the world of information technology, the problem looks ridiculously simple. But the industry has been asleep at the switch.
The millennium bug is caused by some computers being unable to read the date 2000. The problem stems from programmers in the 1970s and 1980s abbreviating years to just 89 or 96.
Under this system 2000 would be abbreviated to 00, and this will be read as an error by computers and cause them to crash or spew out false information.
Surely a trivial sounding problem like this can be cured simply and quickly?
Wrong.

"Peripheral it ain't, that's for sure. It's really central," said Dr Margaret Joachim, Year 2000 coordinator at Electronic Data Systems Corp of the U.S. EDS handles data processing for some of the world's biggest corporations.
Far from presenting corporations with a simple fix, the millennium bug will soak up unprecedented amounts of reprogramming and threatens some businesses with bankruptcy.
Some experts say the damage caused at the turn of the century could be enough to trigger a global recession.

"It's a huge problem. We calculate that the global cost of software changes is between $300 billion and $600 billion worldwide. And we are at the conservative end. Some estimates put this at over $1 trillion," said Nick Jones, research director at the Gartner Group.
Gartner is a technology research firm based in the United States.
Jones said that the millennium bug could be a problem in microprocessors embedded in cars, watches, and home appliances.

And even though industry across the world is cranking up to try to rectify the problem, it can't be sure that all computer programmes at risk will be corrected. Some older mainframe computers have deep layers of different programmes with massive amounts of often opaque instructions.

"It's a needle in a haystack problem. It's difficult to predict, but I wouldn't want my life depending on a computer at that time (midnight, December 31, 1999). I won't be in a plane for instance," Jones said.
Malcolm Munro, senior lecturer in Computer Science at Durham University in northeast England agrees there is a risk that all the faulty computer codes won't be discovered.
"They're not going to find all the occurrences where dates are stored in programmes. Some are buried deep in systems."

But Munro has some sympathy for the programmers responsible. In the 1970s and '80s computers were relatively underdeveloped and space for data was at a premium -- hence the need to abbreviate years. Programmers believed that, as the industry was so fast-moving, this would not be a problem in 2000.
Some businesses are more vulnerable than others.

"Banks, insurance companies, financial services companies and supermarkets, they all need to take decisions based on dates. They will face the biggest problems; some have started seeing problems already," Munro said.
Pharmaceuticals companies are already finding problems as drug expiry dates are stamped 2000 -- and the computer reads this as 1900 and rejects the item as being 96 years old.
Manufacturing companies are thought to be at low risk.
As the huge potential for corporate disaster becomes clearer, banks and accountants are getting nervous.
"Banks won't lend you money unless they are convinced that your business has addressed possible millennium bug problems," said Gartner's Jones.
"Accountants may qualify your annual report if they feel you are vulnerable to this," he said.
And many businesses will feel the heat before the witching hour, as insurance policies and other deals reach up to 2000.

"There will be a rising rate of failure. It will increase in small steps at the end of every quarter and more at the end of years," said Paul Weller of Chase Software, which offers 2000 bug solutions.
"There will be an exponential rate of computer failure between now and the year 2000," Weller said.
As the 2000 bug problem looms larger, conferences are being organised to spread the word and galvanise industry to action.
Robin Guenier, executive director of Taskforce 2000, worries that the message is not getting across.
"We are not making enough progress. We are not getting to senior management," Guenier told a conference this month.
Guenier is taking precautions of his own for midnight on December 31, 1999.

"I shall make sure I'm deep in a cellar somewhere, as far way from any computers as I can get," he said. "And it will be somewhere hot, and I will have flown in at least a month before New Year's Eve."
